title: Now is the time
hook: listen, friends: now is the time to serve the holy and earn the Name (Gauri Purbi M5, ang 13)
tomorrow: A wedding song at a funeral

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first line of hymn five, and your line: karau benantee, I make a request. Did you ask for something as a friend would? Today, what the request actually is. Day four hundred thirty-three.

A market town in Punjab, four hundred years ago. Traders arrive with goods, spend a few days selling and buying, and then the caravan leaves. Everyone knows the rule: what you earn here is what you carry home. If you spend the market days sleeping, or gambling, or arguing, you go home with empty bags. Guru Arjan's listeners knew that world well. Many of them were traders and farmers. So when the last hymn of Sohila explains its urgent request, it reaches for the language of the marketplace: profit, earning, a short stay.
screen: `A MARKET TOWN, A SHORT STAY.` → `WHAT YOU EARN, YOU CARRY HOME.` → `THE HYMN SPEAKS LIKE A TRADER.`

segments.voice: Here's the request, in paraphrase. Listen, my friends: this is the time to serve the holy. Earn the profit of God here, and your dwelling hereafter will be easy. The word for profit is laahaa, an ordinary trader's word, gain at the end of the day. Then the urgency. In paraphrase again: day and night, life is running down; O mind, meet the Guru and set your affairs in order. That's a sentence anyone with a deadline understands. The hours are going whether you use them or not. The hymn goes on: this world is caught in corruption and doubt; the one who knows God crosses over. Buy what you came here to buy. Through the Guru, God comes to dwell in the mind, and you reach your own true home in ease, with no more coming and going. And then the very last request in the whole of Sohila. Guru Arjan, who compiled the scripture, asks for one thing. In paraphrase: Nanak, Your servant, begs for this happiness: make me the dust of the feet of the holy. So the night prayer ends on humility, the lowest place in the room, chosen on purpose. Here's why it belongs at bedtime. Night is when you count the day. What did I earn? Not money: kindness, attention, remembering. The hymn doesn't scold. It just says the market's still open. Tonight counts. Now is the time.
screen: `LAAHAA: THE DAY'S PROFIT.` · `DAY AND NIGHT, LIFE RUNS DOWN.` · `BUY WHAT YOU CAME TO BUY.` · `MAKE ME THE DUST OF THE HOLY'S FEET.` · then, large: `NOW IS THE TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one kind act before bed. Sit for a moment first and let one person come to mind: someone at home, someone you could text, someone you owe a thank-you. Decide one small thing you can do for them tonight. Fill a water glass. Leave a note. Send three warm words. Wash a dish that isn't yours. Picture yourself doing it. Then, when the bell ends, go and do it, before the day closes. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once first. The bell holds the time.
Now is the time. Guru Arjan's request in Sohila's last hymn: listen, friends, life is running down day and night, so serve the holy and earn the profit of the Name today.
Your line: now is the time. Tonight, before you sleep, ask yourself the trader's question: what did I earn today that I can carry home? Day four hundred thirty-three.

screen: `DAY 433 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A WEDDING SONG AT A FUNERAL.`

howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn as the last of Kirtan Sohila every night, so its call that now is the time to serve and remember is often the final teaching heard before sleep.

fork.setup: you're a trader with a few days in the market town before the caravan leaves. what does the hymn tell you to do?
options: earn the profit that lasts while you're here.
fork.reveal: this is the time to serve the holy; earn God's profit here, and the dwelling hereafter will be easy.

original.note: Gurmukhi: seva, selfless service; the hymn asks that now be the time to serve the holy.

trapdoor: what you thought: now is the time is a motivational slogan.
what it means: life is running down day and night, so serve the holy and earn the lasting profit of the Name today.
what a scholar hears: Guru Arjan's hymn uses mercantile terms (laahaa, bihaajhahu, buy) and ends on dhoor, asking to be the dust of the holy's feet.

sources.ref: Gauri Purbi M5, Ang 13 (Kirtan Sohila, hymn 5)

Confirm.
Note that 'sant tahal' is rendered 'serve the holy'; the carry and practice tie this to seva. Confirm.
